articles.title: The Pallidothalamic Tract in Functional Neurosurgery: A Systematic Review.
articles.authors: Al-Smadi MW, Al-Khafaji YQ, Aslan S et al.
articles.abstract: The pallidothalamic tract (PTT), formed by convergence of the ansa lenticularis and fasciculus lenticularis at Forel's field H1, is a major basal ganglia efferent pathway and an emerging functional neurosurgical target. No systematic review has previously synthesised outcomes across PTT-targeted interventions. This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251248260). PubMed, OVID, and Web of Science were searched for studies reporting functional neurosurgical outcomes targeting the PTT or Forel's fields. Prospective and retrospective studies, case series, and case reports were eligible. Methodological quality was assessed using design-appropriate risk-of-bias tools. Forty studies encompassing 483 patients (1966-2025) were included across five modalities: MR-guided focused ultrasound (n = 143), radiofrequency ablation (n = 167), deep brain stimulation (n = 40), cryogenic lesioning (n = 82), and oil-wax injection (n = 52). Mean follow-up was 21 months. In Parkinson disease (PD; 11 studies; n = 135), mean Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale-III improvement was 39%, with reductions in dyskinesia (Unified Dyskinesia Ratings Scale 90%) and tremor (75%). In dystonia (12 studies; n = 87), Burke Fahn Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale and TWSTRS improved by 57% and 47%, respectively. Dual-target strategies, particularly PTT-VIM combinations, showed additive effects, including greater tremor reduction (77%) and improved rigidity. In drug-resistant epilepsy (6 studies; n = 157), seizure reduction occurred in 71% and seizure freedom in 33%. PTT-targeted interventions yield meaningful motor improvements in PD and dystonia, with preliminary evidence supporting additive dual-target benefits. Seizure-reducing effects in refractory epilepsy have been reported. Evidence remains limited by small uncontrolled studies, heterogeneous outcomes, and inconsistent adverse-event reporting. Prospective trials will elucidate the efficacy, safety, and clinical role of the PTT in neurosurgery.

articles.title: Management of fragile X-associated tremor ataxia syndrome: a review for clinicians.
articles.authors: Hall DA, González DA, Klusek J et al.
articles.abstract: Fragile X-associated tremor ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) is a multi-faceted and progressive neurodegenerative disorder that manifests clinically with action tremor, gait ataxia, parkinsonism, peripheral neuropathy, and cognitive and psychiatric features. The disease is highly heterogeneous and there are no FDA approved medications for FXTAS as a specific indication. As such, treatment is symptomatic and must be tailored to the specific needs of a given patient. This review provides expert opinion-based treatment recommendations for the core and ancillary clinical features of FXTAS. Movement disorders, such as tremor, ataxia and parkinsonism may respond to symptomatic medications and therapies, but caution is required when considering surgical interventions such as deep brain stimulation. Cognitive decline can be responsive to medications developed for other cognitive disorders, but these medications work best when combined with non-medication based approaches and all patients should be screened for other reversible causes of memory decline. Psychiatric symptoms, including anxiety, depression, and psychosis, can be treated with psychotherapy and medications; but caution is required to avoid exacerbating clinical and subclinical movement disorder features with psychotropic medications. Rehabilitative therapies, such as speech therapy, occupational, and physical therapy, often enhance patient function and quality of life. Exercise and good nutrition are recommendations that are common to other cerebellar ataxias and adult neurodegenerative disorders and may have a positive impact on general health. A multi-disciplinary approach is recommended to address all components of FXTAS.

articles.title: Peripheral Nerve Stimulation for Essential Tremor: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effectiveness and Safety.
articles.authors: El-Moslemani M, Abbas A, Sabet H et al.
articles.abstract: Essential tremor (ET) is the most prevalent movement disorder worldwide. There are limited current pharmacological therapies, and their side effects often preclude adequate doses. Surgical therapies, such as Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) and Focused Ultrasound (FUS), are reserved for patients with tremor that debilitates activities of daily living (ADLs). Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS), including transcutaneous afferent patterned stimulation (TAPS) and transcutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation (TPNS), has emerged as a promising non-invasive neuromodulatory approach for many patients with intermediate symptoms. A systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conducted, with searches across PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, and Web of Science. Studies enrolling patients with ET assessing TAPS and TPNS were included. Primary outcomes were tremor severity (TETRAS performance scale, total TETRAS) and tremor amplitude. Secondary outcomes included functional disability (BF-ADL, TETRAS-mADL) and safety. Nineteen studies (2,541 patients) were included. Sham-controlled analyses showed statistically significant improvement in TETRAS performance scale scores (MD = - 1.00; p = 0.002; I<sup>2</sup> = 0%). BF-ADL scores improved significantly in sham-controlled analyses (MD = - 1.69; p < 0.0001) and single-arm pre-post analyses (MD = - 3.22; p < 0.0001). Tremor amplitude and total TETRAS outcomes were inconsistent, with high heterogeneity (I<sup>2</sup> up to 94%) driven mainly by differences in assessment timing; the pooled total TETRAS estimate was not statistically significant (p = 0.16). Adverse events were mostly mild and transient; skin irritation was the most frequently reported (7.88%), and no serious adverse events were attributed to the intervention. PNS consistently improved functional outcomes with a favorable safety profile in ET patients. These findings support PNS as a viable adjunctive or on-demand non-invasive therapeutic option, particularly for medication-refractory patients or those unsuitable for surgery.

articles.title: Feeding dystonia in familial chorea, emphasis on VPS13A disease (chorea-acanthocytosis): Clinical course and a scoping review.
articles.authors: Kyhle Jensen J, Rubin C, Halawa I et al.
articles.abstract: Feeding dystonia (FD), a rare phenomenon with involuntary tongue protrusion while eating, is considered a hallmark of VPS13A disease (chorea-acanthocytosis). Here we provide longitudinal data on the natural history of FD, dysphagia and orofacial features among patients with VPS13A disease and other familial chorea syndromes at a tertiary center in Sweden. We also present data on FD in VPS13A disease from a literature search. Clinical data and swallowing assessments on eight patients were reviewed: five with VPS13A disease, two with XK disease (McLeods syndrome) and one with Huntington's disease (HD). A scoping review on the frequency of FD, its treatment and other orofacial manifestations in VPS13A disease was performed. In the cohort, a new patient with VPS13A disease is reported. FD was present in 5 patients; it resolved spontaneously in 2 and was progressive in 2 others. Variable dysphagia occurred in all; all but two with VPS13A disease had a gastrostomy and botulinum toxin injections in the tongue base attenuated FD in two. Weight loss was common and biting of the tongue and lips affected half of the patients; two patients with VPS13A disease died during the follow-up. In our literature search, FD was present in 14.7% of VPS13A cases and its treatment modalities, including deep brain stimulation (DBS), sparsely reported. FD ranges from mild to disabling and is detrimental to nutrition in this longitudinal assessment in VPS13A disease. FD seems to be uncommon in our search but likely underreported and treatment options are limited.

articles.title: Cryoprobe to current practice: neurosurgical legacies of Dr. Irving S. Cooper in movement disorders.
articles.authors: Fisher K, Tsirelman K, Baweja SS et al.
articles.abstract: Before the advent of levodopa therapy for Parkinson's disease, surgical lesioning of the motor thalamus or globus pallidus represented the primary therapeutic intervention for Parkinson's disease and essential tremor at a time when effective medical alternatives were severely limited. In this context, Irving S. Cooper directed one of the most prolific and controversial lesioning practices of the mid-20th century, performing thousands of procedures and documenting outcomes. Through chemopallidectomy, chemothalamectomy, and later cryosurgical techniques, Cooper investigated the relationship between basal ganglia targets and motor symptoms, establishing reproducible symptom-anatomy associations for tremor and rigidity. Cooper's work introduced a systematic approach to target selection that contrasted with earlier lesioning methods. His outcomes demonstrated alleviation of tremor and rigidity when lesions were accurately placed, while highlighting risks of bilateral procedures. Most notably, the cryogenic "test-freeze" method allowed reversible intraoperative physiological inhibition, enabling assessment of clinical benefit before permanent lesions. Although many techniques were later abandoned, principles derived from Cooper's work continue to shape contemporary practice. Modern neuromodulation strategies, including deep brain stimulation and MR-guided focused ultrasound, rely on symptom-based targeting paradigms established during the lesioning era. This vignette examines how Cooper's innovations informed modern targeting strategies and standards of safety in functional neurosurgery.

articles.title: Deep brain stimulation for arm tremor: one-year blinded follow-up of a randomized trial.
articles.authors: Kvernmo N, Reich MM, Roothans J et al.
articles.abstract: To present the secondary endpoints at one-year blinded follow-up from our randomized controlled study, that compared the efficacy of DBS in the ventral-intermediate thalamic nucleus (VIM) with the posterior subthalamic area (PSA) three months each in crossover design, and showed significantly greater reduction of the Sum dominant arm tremor score (Fahn-Tolosa-Marin) during the PSA-DBS period. The outcomes at one year are now reported to verify target choice and sustained benefit with clinically optimized free programming. Forty-five patients with isolated or combined arm action tremor received four-level DBS leads to reach both VIM (upper two levels) and PSA (lower two), and were randomized post-operatively to VIM-DBS month 1-3 followed by PSA-DBS month 4-6, or vice versa. Thereafter electrode choice was free as judged by best clinical outcome. Predefined secondary endpoints were the tremor score improvements from preoperative to the one-year follow-up for dominant and non-dominant arm, other body regions, total score, two patient-rated measures and adverse events. At the one-year follow-up, Sum dominant arm tremor scores had improved from median 24 at baseline to 4 (p<.001, n = 43), corresponding to median 79% improvement. All other secondary endpoints also improved significantly (p<.001). Median action tremor improvement was for Essential tremor(ET) 83%, for Parkinson´s disease(PD) and Dystonic tremor 100% and for Cerebellar tremor 55%. Over 90% of stimulated contacts were in PSA. At one year, good and sustained tremor suppression from PSA-DBS was confirmed in ET, PD and Dystonic tremor. Suppression of Cerebellar tremor was more variable. NCT03156517, May 29, 2017.

articles.title: Documented pain phenotypes and interventional pain-care exposure in patients with dystonia: a retrospective text-mining cohort study.
articles.authors: Shemesh SZ, Fay-Karmon T, Kelmer P et al.
articles.abstract: Pain is a non-motor manifestation of dystonia, but its anatomical heterogeneity and treatment exposure are incompletely characterized. We described pain phenotypes in patients with dystonia referred to a tertiary pain service. In this retrospective cohort study, electronic health record text from 2010 to 2026 was collapsed from 108,797 raw rows to 1860 encounters among 129 patients. A Hebrew-English rule-based pipeline identified pain phenotypes and documented treatment exposures. A category-stratified random sample of 129 records was manually audited by a senior neurosurgeon blinded to pipeline output. The primary objective was phenotype distribution; treatment exposures and phenotype-treatment associations were secondary or exploratory. Mean age was 67.0 years (SD 6.0), 61 patients (47.3%) were men, mean age at dystonia onset was 60 years, and all patients had at least four years of documented disease. Phenotype-codable pain was identified in 125 patients (96.9%). The most frequent phenotypes were limb/extremity (72.9%), spine/radicular (72.1%), cervico-occipital (53.5%), neuropathic-descriptor (43.4%), and myofascial/muscle pain (37.2%). At least one prespecified interventional procedure category was documented in 86 patients (66.7%). Cervical dystonia was associated with cervico-occipital pain (69.4% vs 43.8%; OR 2.91, 95% CI 1.38-6.18; P = .006). Treatment associations were interpreted as co-documentation patterns affected by indication bias. Pain in this referral-enriched cohort was anatomically and mechanistically heterogeneous and frequently accompanied by documented procedural and medication exposure. The findings support prospective assessment using validated pain instruments, but do not establish diagnoses, treatment efficacy, or population prevalence.

articles.title: Genetic Etiologies of Dystonia with Anarthria/Aphonia.
articles.authors: Ménétrey A, Rayco E, Abarghouei ME et al.
articles.abstract: Dystonia with anarthria and/or aphonia (DAnAp) represents a distinctive phenotype manifesting across lifespan. Frequently associated with genetic disorders, early recognition is critical for diagnosis and management. To provide practical recommendations for the clinical evaluation of patients with DAnAp, enhancing recognition and facilitating targeted diagnostic workup. We retrospectively reviewed patients with dystonia and anarthria/aphonia due to established genetic causes across the lifespan at The Hospital for Sick Children and Toronto Western Hospital. Demographic, clinical, genetic, and neuroradiological data were reviewed. Cases were categorized based on the age of onset of neurological symptoms: neonatal (0-4 weeks), infantile (4 weeks - 1 year), early childhood (1-8 years), late childhood/adolescence (8-18 years) and adulthood (>18 years). Fifty-four patients were included, with a mean age of 15.8 years at last assessment (range: 17 months-53 years). We identified 39 distinct genetic etiologies including channelopathies, G-protein-related disorders, developmental and epileptic encephalopathies and metabolic disorders. Most (92%) presented before the age of 8 years, with symptom onset in infancy (37%), early childhood (32%) and neonatal period (24%); only four presented later. Early-onset cases demonstrated more severe phenotypes, including global developmental delay (100% of neonatal cases), seizures (54% of neonatal cases) and absent speech acquisition. Therapeutic interventions included deep brain stimulation in 12 patients, targeted gene or disease-specific therapies were available for three patients in our cohort. Dystonia with anarthria/aphonia is genetically heterogeneous and predominantly early-onset, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment. Early genetic diagnosis is essential to guide management as targeted therapies emerge.

articles.title: Is Unilateral Focused Ultrasound Thalamotomy as Effective and Safe as Unilateral Deep Brain Stimulation for Essential Tremor? - A critical evaluation.
articles.authors: Blomstedt Y, Awad A, Philipson J et al.
articles.abstract: Focused ultrasound (FUS) thalamotomy has become a common surgical treatment for essential tremor (ET), in some settings partially replacing deep brain stimulation (DBS). However, no randomized comparative studies have been performed. A review directly comparing unilateral FUS thalamotomy and unilateral DBS is therefore warranted. A systematic literature search identified studies of thalamotomy FUS or thalamic DBS for ET. Eligible studies reported mean values for predefined items of the Clinical Rating Scale for Tremor (CRST) at 6-12 months follow-up. Studies with long-term outcomes (≥5 years) were also considered. Duplicate or overlapping cohorts were excluded. Thirteen short-term FUS studies (427 patients) and six DBS studies (307 patients) met inclusion criteria. Mean age was comparable, though the FUS cohort showed greater gender imbalance. Improvement in total CRST scores did not differ significantly between FUS and DBS (53% vs. 56%). DBS was associated with significantly greater improvement in contralateral hand tremor (86% vs. 72%), combined hand tremor and function (82% vs. 59%), and activities of daily living (71% vs. 65%). Long-term data were limited: two FUS studies (66 patients) and two DBS studies (36 patients) met criteria. Adverse event profiles differed substantially, with complications more frequent and more often persistent following FUS. Both treatments provide clinically meaningful tremor reduction, though DBS appears to offer greater overall improvement. Permanent side effects after FUS are relatively common but mostly mild. Randomized trials comparing DBS and FUS are needed, particularly regarding side effects and quality of life.

articles.title: Preoperative Functional Imaging Predicts Deep Brain Stimulation Outcome in Craniocervical Dystonia.
articles.authors: Fan H, Boutet A, Elias GJB et al.
articles.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
articles.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established treatment for craniocervical dystonia (CCD), yet postoperative benefit varies widely and cannot be estimated before surgery. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has shown prognostic value across DBS indications. The objective of this study was to develop and externally validate preoperative rs-fMRI models estimating DBS response in CCD. Forty-two patients from two independent centers underwent preoperative 3 T rs-fMRI (discovery, n = 26; validation, n = 16). Using 12 literature-informed, symptom-relevant regions of interest, we quantified the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation as a measure of intrinsic regional neural activity. We applied regularized modeling to classify super-responders, distinguish responders from non-responders, and estimate improvement in Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale motor subscore. When applied to the validation cohort, the imaging models achieved a three-category classification accuracy of 75.0% (50.5%-89.8%) using a sequential two-step procedure (P<sub>perm</sub> = 0.002). Predicted continuous improvement was also correlated with empirical improvement (R<sub>ext</sub> = 0.65, Q<sup>2</sup> = 0.34, P<sub>perm</sub> = 0.004). Within the discovery cohort, nested leave-one-out-cross-validation, in which feature selection and decision-threshold derivation were repeated independently within each training fold, yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.73 (0.50-0.96) and 0.77 (0.51-1.00). Across models, baseline primary motor cortex activity was consistently associated with diminished postoperative benefit. Preoperative rs-fMRI captures clinically relevant variation in baseline brain state in CCD, with predictive performance supported in an external validation. These findings provide preliminary support for rs-fMRI as a potential source of information to aid patient counseling and clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

articles.title: Unilateral MR-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy thalamotomy for refractory multiple sclerosis tremor: 12-month outcomes in four patients.
articles.authors: Aubignat M, Tir M, Ouendo M et al.
articles.abstract: Tremor affects many people with multiple sclerosis (MS), is frequently disabling and responds poorly to medication. Deep brain stimulation, gamma-knife radiosurgery and MR-guided focused ultrasound are options, but each has constraints. MR-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT) is a hardware-free stereotactic thalamotomy providing real-time thermometry, its role in MS tremor is unknown. To describe 12-month clinical, safety and imaging outcomes after unilateral MRgLITT thalamotomy for refractory MS tremor. Single-centre, consecutive case series of four patients with medically refractory MS tremor who underwent robot-assisted unilateral MRgLITT thalamotomy. The primary outcome was the treated-limb Fahn-Tolosa-Marin Tremor Rating Scale (FTM-TRS) at 12 months, scored from standardized videos by a blinded neurologist. Secondary outcomes were patient-reported tremor severity, tremor-related quality of life, adverse events, cognition, mood and MRI lesion characteristics. Analyses were descriptive. The cohort comprised three secondary-progressive and one relapsing-remitting patient (median EDSS 5.5; median tremor duration 15.5 years). The mean treated-limb FTM-TRS score fell from 15.8 to 5.5 at 12 months (mean per-patient reduction 65.7%, range 41.2-80.0%). Quality of life improved in three of four patients. Acute adverse events occurred in two patients (transient gait ataxia; transient hemiparesis with dysarthria), both resolving by 3 months, none persisting at 12 months. Cognitive decline in one patient and mood deterioration in two, the causes of these changes remain uncertain. Unilateral MRgLITT thalamotomy was feasible and produced meaningful, largely sustained tremor reduction within a narrow therapeutic window. Larger controlled studies are required to establish efficacy, durability, safety and function.

articles.title: Clinical Reasoning: A 13-Year-Old Boy With Acute-Onset Generalized Dystonia, Rostrocaudal Gradient, and Severe Bulbar Dysfunction.
articles.authors: Zhao Y, Wei L, Yi Z et al.
articles.abstract: A 13-year-old adolescent boy developed progressive generalized slowness over 1 month, followed by 10 days of rapidly worsening speech loss, dysphagia, rigidity, and dystonic posturing. Acquired evaluations, including CSF, infectious studies, autoimmune encephalitis panels, and brain MRI, were unrevealing, and empirical corticosteroid/antiviral therapy produced no meaningful improvement. Examination showed severe generalized dystonia with a rostrocaudal severity distribution, prominent bulbar and upper limb involvement, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus, and bilateral Babinski signs. Symptomatic medication produced only a partial reduction of painful paroxysmal episodes without meaningful functional recovery. The patient later underwent bilateral centromedian-parafascicular complex (CM-Pf) deep brain stimulation with limited functional response. This case illustrates how rostrocaudal severity distribution and bulbar dysfunction can redirect the diagnostic approach from acquired encephalitis-like disorders toward early genetic testing.

articles.title: Intraoperative asymmetry of thalamic stimulation mapping in Essential Tremor: specificity of first hemisphere implantation and transitory lesioning effect.
articles.authors: Bucciarelli V, Vogel D, Coste J et al.
articles.abstract: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) effectively reduces symptoms in Essential Tremor (ET). Clinical benefit depends on modulation of distributed neural circuits with still undeciphered mechanisms. Furthermore, the lesioning effect observable intraoperatively following the implantation of the DBS lead in the first brain hemisphere has received little attention. We hypothesize that hemispheric differences exist in the spatial organization of improvement and adverse effects, related to the sequential implantation of electrodes and a transitory lesioning effect. We investigated this hemispheric asymmetry with a data-driven, probabilistic mapping approach, linking simulated stimulation volumes [Volumes of Tissue Activated (VTAs)] to symptom improvement (imp) and side effects (se) for each hemisphere. Intraoperative data from 23 ET patients undergoing DBS lead implantation in the ventrointermediate nucleus of thalamus (Vim) were retrospectively analyzed. The left hemisphere was systematically implanted first. Stimulation spots (positions) were categorized using therapeutic window values and side effect occurrence. Hemisphere-specific probabilistic effect volumes of imp (PVimp) and se (PVse) derived from VTAs, and clusters of stimulation spots grouped by category were computed. They were topographically analyzed in relation to structures of the Vim region, and compared within hemispheres and across hemispheres. In the first implanted hemisphere, PVimp was in the infero-posterior part of Vim reaching the subthalamic tegmental fields, whereas the PVse was above, posterior and lateral to the PVimp, spanning Vim and the ventrocaudal nucleus of thalamus (VC). In the right one, PVimp and PVse overlapped, intersecting Vim and VC, in the intermediate part of both. The stimulation spots clusters, in the left hemisphere, were located around the intermediate part, slightly lateral of Vim and VC to a lesser extent. In the right one, they were located in the intermediate and superior parts of Vim. Significant hemispheric asymmetries were observed, revealing a lesioning effect subsequent to the first DBS lead implantation in the left hemisphere. This led to a broader distribution of optimal positions with a larger PVimp largely overlapping with the PVse in the contralateral right hemisphere. The combined mapping and categorization framework yields hemisphere-specific insights on the transitory lesioning and bi-hemispheric modulation which could guide future DBS strategies.

articles.title: Brain Stimulation as a Treatment for Apathy: A Scoping Review of Effects and Safety.
articles.authors: Grewal P, Seidman MB, Chasen J et al.
articles.journal: The Journal of neuropsychiatry and clinical neurosciences
articles.abstract: Apathy is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by impairment of goal-directed behavior, cognition, and emotional responsiveness. In this scoping review, the authors evaluated the literature on brain stimulation for the treatment of patients with apathy across diagnostic categories and provide recommendations to guide future research and practice. The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, and PsycInfo for studies involving brain stimulation for apathy as a primary or secondary outcome. From 1,209 records, 52 studies evaluating brain stimulation were included; of these, 10 systematic reviews or meta-analyses were synthesized separately. Modalities included repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS; N=26), deep brain stimulation (DBS; N=7), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; N=6), electroconvulsive therapy (N=1), transcranial alternating current stimulation (N=1), and transcranial pulsating electromagnetic field therapy (N=1). Populations included patients with schizophrenia (N=477), Parkinson's disease (PD; N=289), depression (N=288), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) (N=210), Huntington's disease (N=42), PD with MCI (N=28), traumatic brain injury (N=28), stroke (N=14), COVID-19 (N=12), and dementia with Lewy bodies (N=6) (total N=1,366). rTMS improved apathy measures, most consistently in AD, with positive trends in depression, MCI, stroke, and schizophrenia. tDCS showed variable effects, with some benefits for schizophrenia. DBS showed mixed results, varying with stimulation location. Observed adverse events were mild and modality specific. Investigations into brain stimulation as a treatment for apathy show some promise. Conclusions were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous study designs, and variable outcome measures. Randomized trials with common validated apathy instruments, standardized stimulation parameters, and harmonized diagnostic measures may help advance the field.

articles.title: Local field potential biomarkers for adaptive deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease: A scoping review.
articles.authors: Khan RA, Imtiaz Ahamed MS, Thomas FJ et al.
articles.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder in the elderly. Conventionally, to combat the symptoms, drugs such as Levodopa and conventional deep brain stimulation (DBS) are routinely used. However, with time, the efficiency of both treatment modalities wears off and accompany side effects. Advocating for the need to explore subsequent management options such as adaptive DBS (aDBS) - a tailor-made DBS promising more personalized and favorable outcomes. The main objective of this review was to explore local field potentials (LFPs) as biomarkers for aDBS in PD. In addition, to investigate any correlations between the LFPs biomarkers, their physiology, and how they affect the quality of aDBS. A literature search was conducted using two primary electronic databases, PubMed and Scopus, which were examined from 2005 to April 2026. The inclusion criteria were set as LFPs within the DBS framework, focusing on biomarkers such as beta, gamma, phase-amplitude coupling (PAC), or oscillatory activity in PD. A narrative data synthesis was conducted to chart and summarize the main findings from the included studies. A total of 73 articles were included in this review. Suppression of exaggerated beta-band oscillations (13- 35 Hz) consistently correlated with improved motor performance and emerged as the most validated feedback signal for adaptive stimulation. Gamma oscillations demonstrated an emerging role in differentiating motor states, while PAC and other low-frequency oscillations remain exploratory, showing promise for integration with multimodal systems. Based on accumulated evidence, biomarkers were categorized into three tiers: Established (beta-band activity), emerging (gamma oscillations), and exploratory (PAC and others). Although DBS has shown marked improvement in symptoms, LFP-based aDBS represents a future toward personalized, precise, and adaptive treatment for PD; clinical usage of aDBS requires standardization and broader validation.

articles.title: STN-SNr co-stimulation in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of motor and freezing-of-gait outcomes.
articles.authors: Kong L, Li P, Bi Y et al.
articles.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
articles.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) and axial impairments often persist in Parkinson's disease despite optimized medication and subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS). We systematically reviewed whether adding substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) stimulation improves motor and FoG outcomes. Following PRISMA 2020 and PROSPERO registration (CRD420261343479), six databases were searched through 1 May 2026. Primary outcomes compared STN-SNr co-stimulation with STN-only stimulation; stimulation-off or baseline comparisons were secondary. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. UPDRS-III and FoG were pooled as mean differences (MDs) and Hedges' g, respectively, accounting for paired data and within-study dependence. Certainty was assessed using GRADE. Ten studies (nine randomized trials and one observational study) included 109 unique evaluable participants; two single-patient case reports were summarized narratively. UPDRS-III showed no between-group difference across seven studies (73 participants; MD - 0.10, 95% CI - 1.01 to 0.81; I² = 0%; low certainty). FoG showed no additional benefit across six studies (86 participants; Hedges' g - 0.23, 95% CI - 1.04 to 0.59; I²_total = 85.6%; very low certainty). Secondary baseline comparisons favored co-stimulation for UPDRS-III (MD - 13.55) and FoG (Hedges' g - 0.60), but did not isolate an incremental SNr effect. Low-certainty evidence suggests no clinically important difference in global motor outcomes, while very-low-certainty evidence does not demonstrate a consistent additional FoG benefit. Improvements versus stimulation-off or baseline cannot establish an incremental SNr effect. Larger phenotype-stratified trials with objective gait endpoints and systematic adverse-event reporting are needed.

articles.title: The effect of physical activity on Parkinson's disease outcomes in patients with bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation: a systematic review.
articles.authors: Betka M, Szlufik S, Koziorowski D
articles.abstract: Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (DBS-STN) is a recognized treatment for advanced Parkinson's disease. While it improves some clinical symptoms, especially bradykinesia and rigidity, it has limited application for late motor symptoms. Moreover stimulation-related motor adverse effects can increase the motor burden. There is a clear need to develop additional therapies that complement deep brain stimulation in controlling late motor symptoms. Physical activity is a commonly used and recommended form of therapy for patients with Parkinson's disease, supplementary to pharmacological therapy. However, there are no clear recommendations including patients after implantation of DBS-STN stimulators in the group undergoing physiotherapy. The objective of this study is to systematically review the literature on physiotherapy interventions for patients who have undergone DBS-STN implantation and their influence on motor outcomes. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, and a total of 10 studies were included. Despite heterogeneous physiotherapy protocols, the main outcomes (balance, postural stability, gait speed, functional mobility) improved consistently, while motor severity scores and cognitive or neurophysiological effects remain underexplored. Current evidence supports the use of physiotheruapy as a potentially effective and safe addition to the management of motor symptoms in patients after DBS-STN. Future trials with standardized physiotherapy protocols and uniform outcome measures are needed to create overall recommendations.

articles.title: An in silico cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic testbed for comparing visual and deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.
articles.authors: Huang CH, Chen WS, Lai JR et al.
articles.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established intervention for Parkinson's disease (PD), whereas the network-level effects of prescribed periodic visual input implemented with 10 Hz base pulses remain uncertain. We developed a conductance-based cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBT) model comprising 11 Hodgkin-Huxley neuronal populations and a prescribed periodic visual-input unit (RET) to compare 130 Hz subthalamic nucleus (STN) DBS with the archived periodic visual-input condition on the same calibrated PD network. Primary conditions used N = 10 independent runs each. Additional analyses included an unpaired 0-5 mA/cm2 DBS-amplitude series, a matched-seed internal-globus-pallidus-to-thalamocortical-relay (GPi→TC) sensitivity analysis at 0.8, 1.0, and 1.2 × nominal coupling (N = 10 per scale), and a matched-seed three-parameter ±20% local sensitivity analysis (N = 5 per parameter-condition cell). DBS reduced the model-internal STN synaptic-current beta measure from 0.0184 ± 0.0060 to 0.0018 ± 0.0004 a.u. (Holm-corrected p = 1.1 × 10-5), whereas periodic visual input increased thalamocortical relay (TC) and reticular thalamic (RE) firing and enhanced cortical pyramidal (PY) gamma (30-80 Hz) and narrowband 38-42 Hz power. Cortical PY firing was 4.86 ± 0.84 Hz in PD, 5.28 ± 0.87 Hz with DBS (p = 0.285 versus PD), and 10.33 ± 0.85 Hz with periodic visual input (Holm-corrected p = 1.18 × 10-10 versus PD). The ampltude series showed a non-monotonic STN response at 1 mA/cm2; from 2 to 5 mA/cm2, mean STN beta values occupied a narrow range of 0.00186-0.00212 a.u. In the GPi→TC analysis, TC spontaneous firing remained 0 Hz in 30/30 runs, and all 750,000 saved voltage samples were finite and subthreshold (-72.06 to -54.74 mV; no 0-mV crossings). Across the three-parameter analysis, DBS raw STN-beta suppression remained 88.9%-95.8%, and periodic visual input increased TC firing 3.70-4.29-fold relative to nominal PD. These findings show persistence across the tested dose, GPi→TC, and three-parameter local domains but do not establish evoked relay fidelity, global parameter robustness, biological mechanisms, or clinical efficacy.

articles.title: Beyond motor recovery: subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation may improve blinking and dry eye symptoms without restoring tear film homeostasis in Parkinson's disease.
articles.authors: Hamzaoğlu EC, Hamzaoğlu V, Ateş U et al.
articles.abstract: To investigate the longitudinal effects of subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) on objective and subjective dry eye parameters in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). This retrospective observational study included 34 patients with advanced PD who underwent STN-DBS. Comprehensive ophthalmic examinations were performed were performed before surgery and at postoperative week 1, month 1, and month 4. Outcome measures included spontaneous blink rate, tear break-up time (TBUT), Schirmer I test, Oxford corneal staining score, and the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI). Longitudinal changes were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE). Spontaneous blink rate increased significantly over time, reaching statistical significance at postoperative month 4 compared with baseline (rate ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.04-1.36; p = 0.014). OSDI scores showed progressive improvement throughout follow-up, with significantly lower scores at postoperative week 1 (p = 0.038), month 1 (p = 0.036), and month 4 (p = 0.002). In contrast, no significant longitudinal changes were observed in TBUT (p = 0.552), Schirmer I test results (p = 0.992) or Oxford corneal staining scores (p = 0.090). STN-DBS was associated with increased spontaneous blinking and significant improvement in subjective dry eye symptoms in patients with PD, whereas objective measures of tear film stability, tear production, and ocular surface integrity remained unchanged during short-term follow-up. These findings may suggest that the ocular benefits of STN-DBS may be mediated primarily through modulation of central neural mechanisms governing blink regulation and symptom perception rather than restoration of peripheral tear film homeostasis. Continued ophthalmic evaluation and conventional dry eye management remain important following STN-DBS.

articles.title: Caregiver Burden and Its Determinants After Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease: A Cross-Sectional Long-Term Follow-Up Study.
articles.authors: Margarido I, Pacheco C, Ramos J et al.
articles.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, leading to increasing functional dependence even after deep brain stimulation (DBS). Although DBS improves motor outcomes, its long-term impact on caregiver burden remains poorly understood. Our aims were to evaluate caregiver burden after subthalamic nucleus (STN)-DBS and identify patient- and caregiver-related factors associated with burden across different postoperative time points. A cross-sectional study of caregivers of PD patients who underwent STN-DBS at a tertiary center, stratified by time since surgery (2-3, 5-6, 10-11, and ≥15 years), was conducted. Caregivers completed the Zarit Burden Interview, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and an investigator-developed questionnaire. Patient clinical data, including the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), Part III, scores, were obtained from medical records. Group comparisons and multivariable regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with caregiver burden. Eighty-eight patient-caregiver pairs were included. Caregivers were predominantly female (62.5%), with a mean age of 60.0 ± 12.3 years. Caregiver burden was mild to moderate but increased independently with longer time postsurgery. Higher burden was associated with younger caregiver age, higher anxiety and depression scores, greater caregiving time, less personal time, and patient-related factors, including dysphagia, dementia, and male sex. Motor severity (UPDRS III, falls, postural instability) was not associated with caregiver burden. Most caregivers considered STN-DBS beneficial and would choose surgery again. Caregiver burden increased with longer time after STN-DBS and was associated with dementia, dysphagia, and caregiver-related factors but not with motor severity. Several associated factors are potentially modifiable, supporting systematic caregiver assessment and targeted interventions as part of long-term PD management.

articles.title: Continuous Subcutaneous Apomorphine as a Temporary Bridging Therapy for Dopamine Dysregulation Syndrome in Patients with Deep Brain Stimulation.
articles.authors: Binder T, Hartig J, Sitzmann L et al.
articles.abstract: Dopamine dysregulation syndrome (DDS) is a challenging complication of dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson's disease and can persist despite subthalamic deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS). We evaluated a temporary bridging concept in which oral dopaminergic medication was replaced by continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion while maintaining DBS. Six patients with STN-DBS and DDS were temporarily transitioned from oral dopaminergic medication to continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion. Treatment success was defined as reduction of DDS below a predefined threshold (<3 characteristic DDS features). Four of six patients (66.7%) no longer fulfilled the operational DDS criteria. Typical apomorphine-related adverse effects occurred in all patients; however, nausea and malaise limited the treatment in two non-responders. In this uncontrolled case series, continuous subcutaneous apomorphine may represent a useful temporary adjunct to STN-DBS for managing DDS in selected patients. Treatment tolerability appears to be a major determinant of success and requires careful patient selection and monitoring.

articles.title: Deep brain stimulation as neuroimmune-metabolic modulation in Parkinson's disease and beyond: tissue response, glial remodeling, and disease modification.
articles.authors: Deng H, Li X, Wang D et al.
articles.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established symptomatic therapy for Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its biological effects extend beyond modulation of abnormal basal ganglia circuitry. This review conceptualizes DBS in PD as a neuroimmune-metabolic intervention acting across the electrode-tissue interface, glial networks, peripheral immunity, and activity-dependent metabolic systems. PD is characterized by convergent immune and metabolic vulnerability. These processes create a disease environment in which electrical stimulation may interact with inflammation, excitotoxicity, bioenergetic stress, and neuronal resilience. We distinguish implantation-related tissue responses from stimulation-induced biological remodeling. Electrode insertion produces acute injury, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, peri-electrode edema, gliosis, and foreign-body responses, which should not be conflated with the effects of chronic stimulation. Active DBS may modulate central cytokine expression, microglial and astrocytic phenotypes, inflammasome activity, astrocytic glutamate transport, and brain-peripheral immune crosstalk. Emerging evidence also suggests a neurometabolic dimension, including changes in regional glucose utilization, PD-related metabolic network expression, oxidative stress, and neurotrophic signaling. However, these effects are context-dependent and influenced by multiple factors. Although preclinical studies support potential neuroprotective mechanisms involving BDNF/TrkB signaling, mitophagy, reduced excitotoxic-inflammatory coupling, and immune-metabolic rebalancing, clinical evidence remains insufficient to establish DBS as a disease-modifying therapy. Future studies should integrate multiple methods such as longitudinal imaging, electrophysiology, immune profiling and metabolomics. DBS should be understood as a symptomatic circuit-based therapy that may also interact with neuroimmune and metabolic processes, while current evidence remains insufficient to establish a disease-modifying role in PD.

articles.title: Directional Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation: An Initial Report of Safety, Tolerability, and Effectiveness.
articles.authors: Beudel M, Herrington TM, Little S et al.
articles.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
articles.abstract: Adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS) is a safe and effective therapy for people with Parkinson's disease (PWP). Utilization of directional aDBS has not been specifically evaluated. The goal is to report the first data on the safety, tolerability, and preliminary effectiveness of chronic, directional aDBS in PWP. A supplemental cohort from the Adaptive DBS Algorithm for Personalized Therapy in Parkinson's Disease Trial received directional aDBS. Participants who were previously receiving stable continuous directional DBS (dDBS) completed an open-label evaluation of two aDBS modes. Seventeen participants were enrolled, with 15 completing directional aDBS evaluation. The prespecified primary endpoint and post hoc success criterion was met for both directional aDBS modes. On-time without troublesome dyskinesia was increased, with a median of 1.2 hours/day in directional dual threshold aDBS mode. Stimulation-related events were similar between dDBS and directional aDBS. All 15 participants chose to continue with directional aDBS chronically. Preliminary data indicates chronic directional aDBS is feasible, tolerable, effective, and safe in PWP. © 2026 The Author(s). articles.title: Disease Duration Differentiates Freezing of Gait Response to Subthalamic and Nigral Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease in an Exploratory Multicenter Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Weiss D, Cebi I, Schütt M et al.
articles.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) belongs to most pressing unmet symptoms in the treatment of Parkinson's disease. To explore whether combined subthalamic and nigral (STN + SNr) deep brain stimulation improves FoG compared with optimized STN stimulation alone; to identify clinical variables associated with therapeutic response. In this exploratory multicenter randomized controlled double-blind trial, we recruited patients from our existing cohorts and randomized them 1:1 to STN or STN + SNr. After baseline, patients were followed with close interim visits (visits 1-5) for 90 days (visit 6). The Freezing of Gait Assessment Course (FoG-AC) was the primary endpoint and was evaluated at P < 0.2 with exploratory intent. Secondary endpoints assessed responder rates, treatment dynamics, predictors of response, and patient preferences. At V6, STN (n = 23) and STN + SNr (n = 22) FoG-AC outcomes did not differ significantly. We identified responders with clinically meaningful FoG improvement in both the STN (n = 7) and STN + SNr (n = 8) groups. In STN + SNr responders, mean disease duration was ~12 years, which was ~4.5 years shorter than in non-responders, but there were no differences in motor and cognitive functions. Treatment dynamics suggested that FoG responders improved slowly and gradually. The STN + SNr responder group showed numerically stronger FoG improvement compared with STN responders. Additionally, 15 STN compared to 10 STN + SNr patients wished to change treatment after the RCT phase and before unblinding. Both STN and STN + SNr treatment was safe. Future trials evaluating adjunctive STN + SNr stimulation should stratify patients by disease duration to optimize outcomes.

articles.title: Does genetic testing remain relevant in advanced Parkinson's disease?
articles.authors: Westenberger A, Endaya NJ, Brüggemann N
articles.abstract: Genetic testing is traditionally emphasized in early-onset or familial Parkinson's disease (PD), leaving its role in advanced disease uncertain. This mini-review explores, from the perspectives of patients, their family members, and clinical researchers, whether genetic investigation remains meaningful once patients reach advanced PD. In large prospective clinical-genetic screening cohorts, roughly one in seven PD patients has genetic PD. Established genotype-phenotype correlations, spanning cognitive trajectory, levodopa responsiveness, and deep brain stimulation outcomes, continue to inform clinical decision-making even at advanced stages. Thus, patients may gain psychological clarity, receive refined prognostic counseling, and become eligible for gene-specific trials or registries. In addition, patients express altruistic motivations, considering the merit of sharing their genetic testing results with their families and the research community. Unaffected relatives may benefit from more precise, penetrance-informed risk assessment, appropriately scaled surveillance, lifestyle counseling, and reproductive planning, particularly as potential environmental modifiers of penetrance and age at onset become better characterized. Researchers rely on genetically characterized advanced-stage cohorts to identify genotype-phenotype relations, modifiers of onset, progression and treatment response, validate biomarkers, and build the large, deep longitudinal datasets required for emerging gene- and pathway-targeted therapies. Collectively, these perspectives argue against a narrow early-disease "window of opportunity" for genetic testing in PD. Rather than becoming obsolete once the disease reaches a more advanced stage, genetic characterization continues to shape individualized care, family counseling, and translational research. Thus, in the future, the challenge should no longer be to justify genetic testing in advanced PD, but to embed it equitably and systematically within standard care and international research infrastructure across the entire disease course.

articles.title: Dopamine amplifies subthalamic long-latency responses to cortical stimulation in patients with Parkinson's disease.
articles.authors: Beyer JC, Cavallo A, Vanhoecke J et al.
articles.abstract: The cortico-subthalamic hyperdirect pathway provides a rapid route for cortical influence over basal ganglia processing and is a key target of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, to what degree dopamine modulates signal transmission along this pathway in humans remains unclear. Using bidirectional cortical and subthalamic electrical stimulation while invasively recording evoked responses in 15 PD patients undergoing DBS surgery, we examined cortico-subthalamic communication across dopaminergic states. Cortical stimulation evoked a short-latency subthalamic response consistent with monosynaptic hyperdirect activation that was preserved across medication conditions. In contrast, longer-latency subthalamic responses showed significant dopaminergic modulation, while cortical responses to subthalamic stimulation remained unchanged. These results reveal a temporal dissociation within the cortex-basal ganglia network, whereby fast cortical transmission is unaffected by dopamine, which in turn amplifies slower network level communication to the subthalamic nucleus. This separation of fast and delayed components provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how dopamine shapes information flow in the cortex-basal ganglia system.

articles.title: Effects of STN-DBS on voluntary facial mimicry in Parkinson's patients: a pilot study.
articles.authors: Scagliotti E, Pirola E, Remore LG et al.
articles.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
articles.abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) causes hypomimia, an early manifestation driven by motor, limbic and basal ganglia dysfunction that impairs nonverbal communication. Traditional clinical rating scales used to assess facial expressivity are subjective, traditional clinical scales are subjective, whereas automated video analysis based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) provides an objective, fine-grained measurement of specific facial Action Units (AUs). Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation (STN-DBS), a widely adopted therapy for PD, modulates basal ganglia circuits, yet its precise effect on facial mimicry remains poorly characterized. This study evaluates how STN-DBS influences voluntary facial expressivity by comparing Stim-ON/Med-ON and Stim-OFF/Med-ON states. 18 PD-patients with STN-DBS were evaluated in two experimental conditions (Stim-ON/Med-ON VS Stim-OFF/Med-ON). Video recordings captured participants reproducing seven voluntary facial expressions (six basic emotions plus neutral). Facial mimicry was quantified using OpenFace 2.0 to extracts AUs intensities according to the FACS system. MDS-UPDRS-III scores improved significantly in the DBS-ON state (p < 0.001), confirming the expected improvement in motor symptoms. Automated FACS analysis revealed emotion-specific differences in AUs, showing reduced mimicry in the Stim-OFF/Med-ON condition, for neutral (AU06, p = 0.042), happiness (AU06, p = 0.034), fear (AU25, p = 0.043), and anger (AU23, p = 0.036). For sadness, AU09 activation was higher in the OFF state (p = 0.021). No significant differences emerged for disgust or surprise. STN-DBS appears to selectively modulate voluntary facial mimicry in PD, enhancing activation of emotion-relevant AUs, and reducing non-pertinent activations for sadness. These findings indicate that STN-DBS influences emotional motor output beyond classical motor control, potentially benefiting nonverbal social interaction.

articles.title: Effects of globus pallidus internus deep brain stimulation on freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease: a prospective short-term single-arm study.
articles.authors: Zhang P, Cao L, Wang T et al.
articles.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a debilitating symptom in Parkinson's disease (PD), often resistant to medication. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has emerged as an effective treatment for advanced PD, while its effect on FoG remains inconsistent. Specifically, the effect of globus pallidus internus deep brain stimulation (GPi-DBS) against FoG is inconclusive, and relevant studies are scarce. To describe the post-operative effect of GPi-DBS on FoG and identify pre-operative predictors of improvement. Forty-six PD patients undergoing GPi-DBS were assessed pre-operatively and at short-term follow-up (a median of 11 months) using the Gait and Falls Questionnaire (GFQ) and a comprehensive Timed Up and Go (TUG) test that quantified five FoG-related TUG indices. The primary outcome was the within-individual change in TUG total time, computed as the pre-operative med-off value minus the DBS-on med-off value. The secondary outcomes were changes of pre-operative med-off vs. med-on (the acute levodopa response) and pre-operative med-off vs. DBS-off med-off (a within-subject negative control for disease progression). Pre-operative predictors of FoG were assessed to predict the within-individual change in the TUG indices by performing forward stepwise Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) regression analysis. At short-term follow-up, FoG measures (the TUG-derived indices and the self-reported GFQ) improved after GPi-DBS. TUG total time decreased by a median of 5.0 s (95% CI 1.5-14.5; FDR = 0.003), and the longest FoG duration by 1.0 s (95% CI 0-3.5; FDR = 0.030); the other three TUG indices improved in the same direction but did not survive correction (FDR 0.064-0.080). Additionally, GFQ total score decreased from a baseline median of 24 to 17 (Hodges-Lehmann median difference 4.0 points; 95% CI 0-8; n = 46; p = 0.036). In the forward-stepwise AIC regression (n = 40), the pre-operative axial levodopa response was the only pre-operative variable retained for the TUG changes; among the four motor components, only the DBS- related change in the axial subscore was significantly correlated with TUG improvement (Spearman ρ = 0.431, 95% CI 0.138-0.654, p = 0.006). Within this single-arm cohort, FoG measures improved over short-term follow-up after GPi-DBS, and greater pre-operative axial levodopa-responsiveness was associated with greater TUG improvement.

articles.title: Frequency-dependent cerebellar circuits independently gate social vocalizations and movement.
articles.authors: Brandenburg C, Srivastava S, Rey Hipolito AG et al.
articles.abstract: Communication depends on precise coordination between motor execution and cognition. Here we reveal that the cerebellum exerts real-time control over social vocalizations in adult mice. Optogenetic activation of excitatory cerebellar output in the superior cerebellar peduncle suppressed ultrasonic vocalizations with frequency-dependent potency while inducing distinct motor phenotypes. Systematic functional mapping across cerebellar regions and cell types revealed that vocal suppression can occur in the absence of overt motor impairment, suggesting selective control of vocal output beyond gross movement disruption. We identified the periaqueductal gray (PAG), a conserved midbrain vocal control center, as a key downstream mediator of this effect. Deep brain stimulation of the PAG rescued vocal deficits in a model of cerebellar dysfunction without rescuing motor incoordination. These findings define a cerebellar-midbrain pathway that gates vocal behavior and demonstrate that targeted therapeutic neuromodulation can selectively restore communication-related output even in the presence of persistent cerebellar-driven motor deficits.

articles.title: Hyperdirect projections from the supplementary motor area mediate subthalamic stimulation effects on movement initiation and inhibition in Parkinson's disease.
articles.authors: Meyer GM, Albares M, Lio G et al.
articles.abstract: In Parkinson's disease, subthalamic deep brain stimulation improves movement initiation but can induce impulsivity. The origin of these effects remains unclear. Here, we test the hypothesis that modulation of automatic response inhibition, an underrecognized process that governs the ability to refrain from reacting, accounts for both effects. Nineteen Parkinson's disease patients were assessed for (i) behavioural changes in a simple Go/NoGo task, ON versus OFF deep brain stimulation, (ii) structural connectivity between the stimulated subthalamic region and the supplementary motor complex and (iii) a previously established electroencephalographic marker of automatic response inhibition (the DMF170). Under stimulation, patients exhibited faster reaction times and increased commission errors. These changes were accompanied by an increase in DMF170 amplitude, which correlated with reaction times. Finally, behavioural changes were associated with stimulation volume overlap with fibres connecting the subthalamic nucleus to the supplementary motor complex. Our findings link improved movement initiation and increased impulsivity under stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus to a shared anatomical and functional substrate, namely the subthalamic nucleus-supplementary motor cortex loop supporting automatic response inhibition.

articles.title: Incidental Finding of an Asymptomatic Perielectrode Cyst After Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease.
articles.authors: Du Four S, Vandamme S, Vanhauwaert D et al.
articles.abstract: Implanted intracerebral devices can lead to infection, hemorrhage, or the formation of fluid-filled cysts. Formation of a perielectrode cyst after deep brain stimulation (DBS) has been reported in a limited number of patients. Additionally, diverse causes and clinical presentations have been associated with these cysts. We present a case of perielectrode cyst formation three months after implantation of a subthalamic nucleus DBS (STN-DBS) for Parkinson's disease (PD). A 59-year-old woman was diagnosed with PD in 2011. In November 2023, the patient underwent staged placement of an STN-DBS without perioperative complications. Immediate postoperative cerebral CT ruled out acute complications. Postoperatively, the patient showed clear clinical improvement, and a substantial reduction in the levodopa dose was achieved (1,500 mg/24 h vs. 250 mg/24 h). There was a significant change in neurocognitive testing three months postoperatively, with a decrease in the Montreal Cognitive Assessment score from 29/30 to 24/30. Follow-up cerebral MRI showed a perielectrode cystic lesion around the left electrode. The patient's clinical status and electrode impedances remained unchanged during follow-up. Serial imaging demonstrated gradual regression of the cyst. Perielectrode cysts after DBS can occur at different locations and at varying postoperative time points. They may present with diverse clinical manifestations or remain completely asymptomatic. Different putative mechanisms and treatment options have been described; however, the paucity of reported clinical cases makes it difficult to speculate on a primary cause.

articles.title: Is it truly patient-centered? Doctor-patient communication in remote programming for Parkinson's disease.
articles.authors: Xu S, Zhang W, Cheng Y
articles.abstract: Patients with Parkinson's disease require frequent programming after deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery to maintain therapeutic efficacy. Although remote programming promises a more patient-centered and accessible healthcare model, the transition from in-person to virtual visits may introduce unique barriers that compromise this innovative care model. From a doctor-patient communication perspective, this study explores these specific communication barriers and their subsequent impact on programming outcomes and patient experience. Non-participatory observation and in-depth interviews were used to understand the experiences of patients, caregivers, and doctors regarding communication during remote programming of DBS. Thematic analysis was applied to analyze the qualitative data. A total of 49 participants were enrolled. Three themes were identified: Structural changes in doctor-patient communication; Expanded patient responsibility; and Weakened emotional support. Findings indicate that Parkinson's patients face new barriers to communication access, heavier burdens of self-expression, and poorer outcomes in emotional communication. The shift in programming models has introduced numerous new challenges for patients and their caregivers, including mastering digital devices, ensuring that home environments are suitable for online consultations, accurately describing symptoms, and accepting the absence of emotional comfort.

articles.title: Levodopa and Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation Modulate Excitation/Inhibition Balance and the Neural Encoding of Isochronous Sequences in Persons With Parkinson's Disease.
articles.authors: Criscuolo A, Schwartze M, Schwarz J et al.
articles.journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
articles.abstract: Temporally regular auditory stimuli, as found in isochronous sound streams, metronome beats, or music, are often used in rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) interventions to initiate and stabilize the temporal coordination of motor plans in persons with Parkinson's disease (pwPD). Research suggests that RAS promotes the recruitment of a cerebellar-prefrontal network and recalibrates abnormal β-band synchronization in the striato-thalamo-cortical pathway. These cuing effects can resemble those observed via dopaminergic treatments (e.g., levodopa) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the subthalamic nucleus (STN). Here, we investigated the influence of both levodopa administration and STN DBS on the neural encoding of isochronous auditory sequences in pwPD. A comprehensive analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) data revealed changes in β-band event-locked neural responses, as well as event-related potentials, neural tracking of rhythm (δ-band inter-trial phase coherence), and excitation/inhibition balance (E/I) as a function of these treatments. Furthermore, we characterized the link between changes in E/I and motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) with levodopa administration. We suggest that characterizing individual responses to specific treatments is a fundamental step in tailoring rehabilitation protocols and optimizing intervention efficacy.

articles.title: Non-motor symptoms burden and motor recovery following STN-DBS in Parkinson's disease: a data-driven longitudinal analysis.
articles.authors: Abbas G, Peach R, Temuulen U et al.
articles.abstract: Subthalamic nucleus-deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) reliably improves cardinal motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, gait disorders and non-motor symptoms (NMS) may persist or emerge following surgery, diminishing quality of life and complicating clinical management. To characterize the dominant axes of clinical covariance across motor and non-motor domains before and after STN-DBS, and to determine whether non-motor symptom severity moderates post-DBS gait and mobility change. 100 PD patients undergoing STN-DBS (mean age 60.2 ± 7.6 years; 67% male) were studied. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on thirteen motor and non-motor sub-scores at pre-DBS, 1-year follow-up (1-y FU), and a subset (n = 33) at 3-5-year follow-up. Moderation was tested using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA): each 1-year motor outcome was regressed on its pre-DBS baseline, a non-motor moderator, and their interaction, adjusting for age and disease duration, with a significant interaction indicating that baseline non-motor severity was associated with the degree of subsequent motor recovery. PCA identified a core motor triad: gait, mobility, and freezing of gait as the primary source of clinical variance at all timepoints (PC1: 35% pre-DBS, declining to 28% at 3-5-y FU), PC1 was the only component to exceed a permutation null (p < 0.001), with memory-related impairment increased at longer-term follow-up. Moderation analysis showed that higher pre-operative mood burden specifically for psychomotor and psychosomatic symptoms were associated with poorer recovery of mobility (Psychomotor β = 1.16, p < 0.05). At 1-y FU anxiety and psychosomatic symptoms showed concurrent associations with mobility and overall motor burden (Anxiety β = 2.30, p < 0.05). STN-DBS outcomes extend beyond global motor improvement and may be shaped by associations spanning the motor, cognitive, and mood domains. Higher NMS baseline burden was associated with poorer mobility recovery, and mood symptoms at follow-up were associated with concurrent motor burden. These exploratory findings support considering multi-domain pre-operative assessment and post-operative mood monitoring, as potential targets for optimizing motor outcomes.

articles.title: Predictive factors associated with interval changes in STN-DBS lead-tip position between immediate and delayed postoperative CT.
articles.authors: Ota T, Fukuda M, Masuda H et al.
articles.abstract: Brain shift during deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery may contribute to changes in lead position. Although intracranial air volume is considered an important factor, other intraoperative factors may also influence lead displacement. This study evaluated interval changes in subthalamic nucleus (STN)-DBS lead-tip position between immediate and delayed postoperative computed tomography (CT) and investigated factors associated with these changes, including intracranial air volume and intraoperative head position. We retrospectively analyzed 42 DBS leads implanted bilaterally in the STN of 21 patients with Parkinson's disease. Lead-tip coordinates were assessed using Elements software (Brainlab) on CT obtained immediately after implantation and after resolution of intracranial air. Interval displacement was defined as the difference in lead-tip coordinates between the delayed and immediate postoperative CT scans. Intraoperative head position was quantified as "Angle A," measured from the horizontal reference line to the anterior commissure-posterior commissure line. Associations between potential explanatory factors and lead-tip displacement were assessed using linear mixed-effects models with patient included as a random intercept to account for within-patient correlation between bilateral leads. Lead-tip positions showed significant interval displacement in the lateral, anterior, and caudal directions. In univariable mixed-effects analysis, intracranial air volume was significantly associated with anterior displacement (β = 0.033, 95% CI 0.018-0.048, p < 0.001), whereas Angle A was not (β = -0.030, 95% CI - 0.067-0.007, p = 0.111). In a multivariable mixed-effects model including intracranial air volume and Angle A, intracranial air volume remained significantly associated with anterior displacement (β = 0.0289, 95% CI 0.0110-0.0469, p = 0.002), while a larger Angle A was associated with less anterior displacement (β = -0.0270, 95% CI - 0.0535 to - 0.0004, p = 0.047). Intracranial air volume was consistently associated with anterior STN-DBS lead-tip displacement between immediate and delayed postoperative CT. Intraoperative head position was also associated with anterior displacement after adjustment for intracranial air volume, although this finding was of borderline statistical significance and should be considered exploratory. These findings support efforts to minimize intracranial air entry during DBS implantation, while the potential influence of intraoperative head positioning requires further prospective investigation.

articles.title: Preoperative neuropsychological prognostic factors for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.
articles.authors: Scarsbrook MW, Vadivelu S, Kolodisner J et al.
articles.abstract: Preoperative neuropsychological evaluation is standard in deep brain stimulation (DBS) candidacy assessment for Parkinson's disease (PD), but batteries vary substantially across centers and may require 6-8 h across multiple visits. To synthesize evidence on preoperative neuropsychological prognostic factors for cognitive, functional, behavioral, speech, and quality-of-life outcomes following DBS and develop an evidence-informed assessment framework. PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched through May 19, 2026. Eligible studies reported an identifiable preoperative neuropsychological measure associated with DBS candidacy or selection or with a postoperative outcome assessed at least 6 months after surgery. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using QUIPS and PROBAST. Evidence certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Thirty-four studies comprising 3783 DBS patients were included. Among 311 extracted results, 238 involved an identifiable prognostic predictor, of which 117 (49.2%) reported adjusted multivariable estimates. Global cognition, executive function, and memory were evaluated as prognostic predictors in 21, 17, and 8 studies, respectively, with generally supportive directions when determinable. MDRS/DRS was most extensively studied but frequently directionally indeterminate, whereas MoCA, semantic/category fluency, and WCST each showed supportive directions in at least two studies. No instrument demonstrated comparative prognostic superiority. Global cognition, executive function, and memory showed generally supportive but low-certainty prognostic associations. Based on these findings and consensus recommendations, we propose a standardized framework incorporating a clinical interview and streamlined testing battery requiring approximately 2 h to improve efficiency, consistency, and comparability across centers.

articles.title: Remote Versus In-Person Follow-up Programming After Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease: A Multicenter Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
articles.authors: Shaik J, Zhang W, Zentsch V et al.
articles.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
articles.abstract: Remote programming of deep brain stimulation may improve access to specialized postoperative care for people with Parkinson's disease, but prospective randomized evidence remains limited. We aimed to determine whether remote follow-up programming after standardized inpatient initiation is noninferior to conventional in-person follow-up programming for motor outcomes during the early postoperative period. In this prospective, randomized, open-label, multicenter noninferiority trial, adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease who recently underwent bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation implantation at six German centers were randomly assigned 1:1 to conventional in-person follow-up programming or remote follow-up programming through a secure telemedicine platform during the first 90 days after surgery. All participants underwent initial in-person postoperative programming before randomization. The primary outcome was the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part III score at 90 days in the medication on and stimulation ON state. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 5 points. Fifty-two participants were randomly assigned. The per-protocol population included 26 participants in the conventional care group and 22 in the remote programming group. The between-group median difference of the primary endpoint was -2.5 points (95% confidence interval, -9.0 to 2.0), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion. Secondary clinical outcomes and patient-reported outcomes were broadly comparable between groups. Serious adverse events occurred at similar frequencies in both groups, and no deaths occurred. Remote follow-up programming after standardized inpatient initiation achieved motor outcomes noninferior to conventional in-person follow-up during the first 3 months, with no clear short-term safety signal. © 2026 The Author(s). articles.title: Research Progress of Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease.
articles.authors: Peng W, Yang Y, Wang J et al.
articles.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where current pharmacological and surgical interventions, including Deep Brain Stimulation, often fail to reverse neuronal degeneration or halt disease progression. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has emerged as a novel, non-invasive neuromodulation technology with significant therapeutic potential. This review synthesizes current research on the key acoustic parameters, biological mechanisms, and clinical applications of LIPUS in PD. Unlike High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), which relies on thermal ablation to destroy target nuclei (e.g., Vim, STN), LIPUS utilizes low-energy mechanical waves (typically <3 W/cm²) to exert non-thermal regulatory effects without damaging tissue. Mechanisms of action include the modulation of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo1), enhancement of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), promotion of autophagy, and regulation of microglial phenotypes to reduce neuroinflammation. We further compare LIPUS with HIFU, highlighting the superiority of LIPUS regarding safety, reversibility, and the absence of requirement for MRI-based thermal monitoring. While preliminary clinical studies using wearable LIPUS devices indicate improvements in motor and cognitive functions, a unified consensus on optimal stimulation parameters and targeting strategies is lacking. Future research should focus on large-scale, standardized clinical trials to establish precise protocols for LIPUS as a disease-modifying therapy for PD.

articles.title: Spectral-spatial Modeling of Neural Couplings in Functional Connectivity of Motor Networks.
articles.authors: Abbaspour H, Wade MH, Hurt CP et al.
articles.abstract: Functional neural connectivity reflects coordinated interactions within brain networks in both health and disease. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is widely used for this purpose, but its pairwise formulations overlook spatially distributed, spectrally correlated structures in neural activity that arises from complex brain circuits. We developed a spectral-spatial generalized linear model (SS-GLM) to characterize the high-frequency response as the integrated outcome of multiple low-frequency phase sources across channels and frequencies. Our method also utilizes a regularization strategy to mitigate predictor collinearity and spurious effects for stable attribution of network-level coupling estimates. Validation was performed using both synthetic data and human motor network recordings from 25 patients with Parkinson's disease undergoing deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery. In synthetic analyses, SS-GLM accurately recovered ground-truth coupling configurations under multiple plausible scenarios. In real data, the framework revealed coherent cortico-subthalamic coupling patterns across distinct motor tasks that aligned with clinically effective DBS contacts and their anatomical organization. Conventional pairwise PAC metrics, such as the modulation index and GLM assess interactions in isolation. In contrast, SS-GLM jointly models distributed predictors and yields spatially localized, spectrally specific coupling estimates that also achieve stronger correspondence with clinical stimulation outcomes. This work offers a principled and extensible framework for advancing functional connectivity analyses, with improved interpretability of network-level interactions, enhanced robustness to confounds, and broad potential for future applications in systems neuroscience and neuro-engineering research.
